rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient that spans nearly the full organic range at a moderate temperature, maximizing the chance all 10 compounds elute within 42 min while revealing the overall elution window and any critical pairs. The mid-length gradient should give useful first-pass resolution without being so shallow that strongly retained compounds risk truncation.

All 10 peaks eluted cleanly by 12.6 min, so the original window is wider than needed; narrowing phi1 should concentrate the gradient over the actual elution region and can improve CRF by reducing run time while keeping all peaks inside the gradient. Holding tG and T fixed isolates the effect of trimming the high-organic end on the critical mid-run cluster around peaks 5–7.

The broad window with tG 20 already gave full resolution, so now test a steeper version to see how much runtime can be cut before the mid-cluster around peaks 5–7 becomes limiting. This slope probe will show whether CRF can be improved mainly by faster analysis while still keeping all 10 compounds resolved.

The key cluster is strongly slope-sensitive: at 20 min all pairs are fine, while at 10 min peaks 5–7 compress too much. An intermediate gradient should retain most of the speed gain while restoring the critical resolution around peaks 5–7, likely improving on the current best CRF.

CRF improved markedly going from 10 to 14 min, and the only remaining weakness is the 6/7 pair at R 1.20, so a slightly shallower gradient is the most direct refinement. Testing 16 min should reveal whether a small extra gain in that critical resolution is enough to push CRF to the maximum without incurring any time penalty.

At 14 min the only deficiency is the 6/7 pair, and that pair may need a selectivity shift rather than more slope change. A modest drop in temperature should slightly increase retention and can alter the close-pair ordering/selectivity enough to improve resolution while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve the excellent CRF.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity in the critical cluster, so probe the opposite direction while keeping the near-optimal slope fixed. A modest increase to 45 C may improve the 6/7 separation enough to raise the resolution term without adding any time penalty.

Temperature moves away from 40 C both worsened the critical selectivity, so stay at 40 C and fine-map the slope around the current optimum. Testing 12 min checks whether a slightly faster run than 14 min can still keep the 6/7 pair sufficiently resolved and possibly improve CRF.

At 14 min and 40 C, all peaks elute by 9.4 min, implying the useful gradient window likely ends well below 0.95; trimming only the high-organic end moderately may improve selectivity in the crowded mid-cluster without pushing the last peak too late. This tests whether a narrower but still broad window can outperform the current best without the severe time penalty seen at phi1 0.65.

The modest trim to phi1 0.85 improved the 6/7 pair enough to beat the previous best, suggesting the optimum may lie between 0.85 and 0.95. Testing phi1 0.90 refines that window and may preserve full resolution with a slightly smaller time penalty than phi1 0.85.

The best two methods indicate the sweet spot is a moderately trimmed high-organic limit, and the time term is already zero at 14/0.90, so the remaining opportunity is to gain speed without collapsing the 6/7 pair. Combining the stronger selectivity of phi1 0.85 with the faster 12 min slope tests whether that narrower window can hold critical resolution while potentially reaching the CRF maximum.

The current optimum is near phi1 0.90 and tG 14, with only the 6/7 pair limiting the resolution term; a slight increase in tG at the same phi window is the cleanest way to see if that pair crosses into full resolution. This tests whether the modest extra spreading can reach CRF 1.000 while keeping the run short enough to avoid a meaningful time penalty.

Around the optimum, changing phi1 improved the critical 6/7 pair more than changing tG, so the remaining path to 1.000 may be a selectivity tweak at the better-narrowed window rather than a longer run. Testing 45 C with phi1 0.85 probes whether temperature and the trimmed gradient together can separate the close pair without introducing a time penalty.

Temperature changes have been highly non-monotonic, but the only unexplored combination close to the current best is lowering T at the best phi1 window of 0.90. This checks whether the favorable window at phi1 0.90 can convert the temperature shift into a small selectivity gain for the 6/7 pair without sacrificing speed.

Temperature is clearly not helping, so the remaining lever near the optimum is the low-organic boundary; the first peak is not close to unretained, so raising phi0 slightly may reshape the effective phi window around the crowded middle cluster. This tests whether trimming the low end while keeping the successful phi1 0.90 and tG 14 can improve the critical selectivity enough to reach the top CRF.

Raising phi0 improved the best method, so the next refinement is to combine that better low-end setting with the slightly narrower high-end window that previously gave the strongest 6/7 resolution. This targets a possible final gain in the limiting pair while likely keeping run time short enough for the time term to stay negligible.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so this is a controlled local probe around the optimum to map robustness rather than chase a higher score. Increasing phi0 one more step tests whether the method sits on a broad optimum or whether 0.10 is the upper useful low-end limit before the critical cluster starts to compress again.

Now that 0.15/0.85/14/40 also gives CRF 1.000, continue stepping phi0 upward to define the breadth of the optimal plateau and find the highest practical starting strength before early peaks approach the dead-time region. This robustness check uses the same successful phi1, tG, and T while exploring how far the low-end trim can be pushed.

The optimum plateau includes phi0 0.15, and pushing phi0 to 0.20 started to compress the first peak toward the void, so hold phi0 at 0.15 and trim phi1 one more step. This checks whether a slightly narrower upper window can maintain full resolution while preserving the zero time penalty and broadening our map of equally optimal methods.

Both phi0 0.10 and phi0 0.15 are on the optimum plateau at phi1 0.85, and phi1 0.80 kept full resolution but introduced a small time penalty at phi0 0.15. Testing phi0 0.10 with phi1 0.80 checks whether a slightly lower start can pull the last peak earlier while preserving the stronger 6/7 separation from the narrower upper window.

With the maximum already achieved, use the remaining injections to map the top ridge around the optimum. This complementary point to the successful 0.15/0.85 and 0.10/0.90 methods will show whether phi0 0.15 with a slightly wider upper window also lies on the 1.000 plateau.

The optimal plateau is centered at phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85 with tG 14, so the only untested nearby direction is a slightly steeper gradient at the best window. This checks whether the improved selectivity from phi0 0.10/phi1 0.85 is strong enough to keep full resolution even at 12 min, which would define the fastest near-optimal method.

Since 0.15/0.85/14/40 is also on the 1.000 plateau, test the steeper 12 min gradient at that neighboring optimum to compare how robust the critical 6/7 pair is versus the 0.10 start. This finishes mapping the fastest variants around the best window while staying close to the known optimum.

We have already secured the maximum CRF, so use one of the last injections to test thermal robustness of the best-performing window rather than slope. This tells us whether the optimum at phi0 0.10, phi1 0.85, tG 14 is tightly tied to 40 C or remains near-optimal with a modest temperature increase.

For the final run, complete the temperature-robustness check of the best method by testing the opposite direction from 45 C. This brackets the optimum and confirms whether the 1.000 method is sharply centered at 40 C or tolerant to lower temperature.
